analysis.one_liner: Pays Members of Congress a tax-free daily allowance for lodging and meals when they travel to Washington to vote.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would give members of Congress a taxpayer-funded per diem for voting trips, sits in committee with no cosponsors and no action since its referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new entitlement for Members of Congress: on any day they record a vote in person in Washington, they could claim a federal per diem for lodging and meals at the same government rates federal employees use, plus the day before and after their travel. The money would not count as taxable income, and DC-area members would be excluded. It has not moved since being referred to the House Administration Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Members of Congress who live outside the Washington area. They could bill the Treasury for hotel and meal costs on every voting day, tax-free, without dipping into their existing office allowances. Members from the DC region get nothing, so the benefit is concentrated on members with longer commutes.

how_it_helps.text: A Member who records a vote in person is entitled to a per diem for Washington-area lodging and for meals and incidentals, at the same rates federal employees receive under General Services Administration rules [S2].
The allowance would also cover the day before and the day after a voting day when the member travels to or from Washington [S2].

The bill directs the House Administration and Senate Rules committees to write rules so the payment is not treated as earned income for federal, state, or local taxes, meaning members keep the full amount [S2].
Members whose designated residence is inside the Washington Metropolitan Area are not eligible, and members cannot claim the per diem for costs already paid from their existing office accounts [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers generally. Every per diem a member claims is a new federal outlay, on top of the member's salary, existing travel allowances, and office expense accounts. The bill does not identify a funding source or cap total spending, so the cost grows with the number of voting days.

drawbacks.text: It creates a new taxpayer-funded perk for members of Congress at a time when members already receive a salary, travel reimbursements, and office expense allowances; the bill adds a second, tax-free payment for costs those existing allowances can cover [S2].
The tax-free design means the public pays more than if the same money were taxed as income, and the bill directs regulators to make that treatment as broad as practicable [S2].
It applies to this Congress and every future one permanently, with no expiration or spending cap [S2].
Members may designate any residence in their district or state as their 'designated residence,' which leaves room for members to choose whichever home maximizes eligibility [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a fair policy argument on one side: federal employees who travel for work get per diems, and members who must physically show up in Washington to vote incur real hotel costs, especially those from distant states. But the bill addresses that at public expense without any offset, cap, or restriction on how often the allowance can be claimed, and it makes the payments tax-free, which increases the cost to the public. The main beneficiaries are sitting lawmakers, not constituents.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Administration Committee, which has taken no further action on it.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Rogers of Alabama introduced the bill on March 31, 2025, and it was referred to the Committee on House Administration [S1].
No other action has been taken since the referral, and no member has cosponsored it [S3], [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained yet. The bill is dormant, so taxpayers are spared the new per diem cost for now, and members of Congress who wanted the allowance have not gotten it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers, for now — the bill is dormant

for.name: Rep. Mike D. Rogers
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a tax-free per diem allowance for members traveling to Washington to vote.

sides.party_line_note: No one has opposed the bill on the record; it simply has no cosponsors and has not moved, so there is no visible partisan lineup yet.

industries.note: The bill would give sitting lawmakers a new tax-free, taxpayer-funded payment for lodging and meals on voting days, on top of salary and existing allowances. Because the benefit flows to officeholders themselves rather than to constituents, the officeholders' interest in this bill runs against the taxpayers who would fund it.

A guaranteed stream of per-diem-funded stays for hundreds of members on voting days would channel new federal money to Washington-area hotels and restaurants, subsidized by taxpayers rather than by the travelers themselves.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors, no committee action months after referral, and no hearing scheduled, the bill shows none of the usual signs of advancement. Member-compensation bills like this typically die quietly in committee, and nothing in the record suggests this one will be different this session.
